medical.title: Half-matched bone marrow transplant expands options for children with severe aplastic anemia
medical.summary: Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center and Johns Hopkins Children's Center report that bone marrow transplant using half-matched family donors achieved a 96% survival rate among child, adolescent and young adult patients with severe aplastic anemia, a rare, life-threatening disorder in which the bone marrow fails to produce enough healthy blood cells. The approach expands access to potentially curative treatment for patients who do not have a fully matched donor.

medical.title: Three-week radiation course a safe option for breast cancer patients undergoing reconstruction, trial shows
medical.summary: Results of a national clinical trial led by the Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology in conjunction with NRG Oncology and the Canadian Cancer Trials Group show that a shorter, three-week radiation schedule following a mastectomy is as safe and effective as the standard five-week treatment for women undergoing breast reconstruction. The results of the RT CHARM trial (Alliance A221505) are published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

medical.title: How trustworthy is AI breast cancer detection? New method gauges uncertainty for individual patients
medical.summary: While AI offers the ability to improve human experts' ability to diagnose and treat diseases like breast cancer, well-publicized errors across the broader AI field are cause for concern. A team from the University of Pittsburgh has used PSC's flagship Bridges-2 supercomputer to design a deep neural network (DNN) that takes uncertainty into account in diagnosing breast scan images.

medical.title: AAO: Association between GLP-1 receptor agonists and age-related macular degeneration explored
medical.summary: Crude odds ratios suggest an increased risk for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in association with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) use, but this finding is reversed after adjustment for cardiometabolic confounding variables, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Ophthalmology, held Oct. 9 to 12 in New Orleans.

medical.title: After stroke and AFib, restoring heart rhythm linked to lower risk of another stroke
medical.summary: For people hospitalized with ischemic stroke and atrial fibrillation (AFib), restoring the heart's normal rhythm within eight weeks after stroke is associated with a lower risk of having another stroke, according to a new study published in Neurology.

medical.title: Newer anticoagulants may help prevent strokes in AFib patients with previous brain bleeds
medical.summary: For people with atrial fibrillation (AFib), an irregular heartbeat, and intracranial hemorrhage, a type of stroke also known as a brain bleed, anticoagulant use was associated with a lower risk of ischemic stroke and death, according to a new study published in Neurology. The study also found no increased risk of more brain bleeds when people took newer anticoagulants.

medical.title: Air pollution and temperature variability are associated with higher blood glucose levels
medical.summary: A European study involving GCAT identifies associations between air pollution, temperature variability and blood glucose levels in people without diabetes.

medical.title: Personalized medicine breakthrough for childhood leukemia
medical.summary: Researchers from Newcastle University and Great Ormond Street Hospital have identified new predictors of relapse in children and young people with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) treated with the immunotherapy drug blinatumomab, as part of a U.K.-wide study.

medical.title: STI rates drop following antibiotic use recommendations for gay and bisexual men
medical.summary: After years of rising sexually transmitted infection (STI) rates in Australia, new Burnet Institute–led research has found promising evidence that an existing antibiotic taken after sex may be helping to reduce syphilis and chlamydia diagnoses among gay and bisexual men.

medical.title: Study finds health care provider photos in waiting rooms can strengthen patient trust
medical.summary: A new Florida State University study finds that adding health care providers' photographs to clinic welcome signs can strengthen certain aspects of patient trust before patients even meet their providers.

medical.title: Pancreatic cancer study highlights body's natural molecules as potential treatment tools
medical.summary: Pancreatic cancer cells are remarkably good at doing one thing: growing. But new Texas A&M research suggests that two tiny molecules already present in the body may help slow them down.

medical.title: Blood proteins could reveal clues to prostate cancer risk more than a decade before diagnosis
medical.summary: Proteins linked to the immune system, cell adhesion, blood vessel formation and known prostate cancer genes were associated with the future risk of developing prostate cancer, including aggressive disease, in a new study led by researchers at Oxford Population Health.

medical.title: Wearable pressure sensor uses cold-spray adhesion method for enhanced health monitoring
medical.summary: In a potential advance for wearable technology, researchers from Virginia Commonwealth University and Florida International University have developed a cold-spray technique that can reliably deposit sensors directly onto human skin and other flexible surfaces.

medical.title: Experimental treatment selectively reduces harmful protein in lab models of rare inherited brain disorder
medical.summary: Researchers from DZNE and the Hertie Institute for Clinical Brain Research (HIH) at the University of Tübingen, together with experts from Bonn, London and Portugal, have developed and successfully tested in human neurons cultured in the lab a new approach for treating the rare neurodegenerative disease spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3).

medical.title: Existing cancer drug reduces blood vessel malformations in the brain
medical.summary: Researchers have identified a substance that reduces blood vessel lesions in the brain in the disease cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM). The substance is already used to treat brain tumors in children and could therefore be repurposed relatively rapidly to treat CCM, hopefully replacing surgery, currently the only treatment option.

medical.title: Tuberculosis vaccine's link to reduced dementia risk gains mechanistic support
medical.summary: Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG), a vaccine widely used to prevent tuberculosis and treat bladder cancer, may also have properties that reduce the risk for dementia, according to new findings in a study of mice. BCG is a live, weakened vaccine made from an altered strain of the bacterium Mycobacterium bovis.

medical.title: 'Digital twins' of immune system in pregnancy identify drugs to prevent early labor
medical.summary: Researchers have identified two common drugs that may, when given together during pregnancy, prevent premature births. The finding is the fruit of a new Stanford Medicine–led, artificial intelligence–powered technique for screening drugs to prevent early labor. It uses a comprehensive atlas of the immune system, which the researchers built to be accurate at a cell-by-cell level, to create "digital twins" of the immune systems of individual pregnant women for virtual drug testing.

medical.title: Modifiable psychosocial factors linked to depression among US cancer survivors
medical.summary: Loneliness, functional limitations and lack of social support were independently associated with depression in a large U.S.-based study of cancer survivors by Philip Baiden from The University of Texas Arlington, U.S., and colleagues, published Oct. 21, 2026, in the PLOS One.

science.title: Japan's expensive funerals and declining birthrates are transforming ancestral traditions
science.summary: Whenever I drive amid the mazelike bustle of Tokyo's Shuto Expressway, where approximately 1 million vehicles transit daily, I see billboard advertisements for all manner of businesses: dentists, hotels, car and tire companies, and affordable funerals. Lots and lots of funerals.

science.title: Salt marshes are proving to be powerful allies in building a climate-resilient coastline
science.summary: Salt marsh sediment and vegetation can remain largely intact even during extreme storm surges. This was demonstrated in a large-scale experiment in which researchers transported sections of salt marsh to an experimental facility capable of producing the world's largest artificial waves. The results show how salt marshes can contribute to natural coastal protection, both in the Netherlands and beyond. The results were published in the journals Nature and Communications Sustainability.

science.title: AI designs functional enzyme components that could help expand drug discovery
science.summary: New active ingredients for drugs to treat infections, cancer or other serious diseases are often based on substances originally discovered in microorganisms, plants or other living organisms. Producing or improving such active ingredients in a targeted manner using microorganisms is often challenging because the underlying biological processes are extremely complex.

science.title: A scuff on your bag, a dent in your mug—and suddenly it feels like time for a new one
science.summary: Imagine you have a bag you really like. It felt like "the one" when you bought it. Over time, it starts to look worn. There are some scuffs on it. Nothing is actually wrong with the bag, and it still works exactly as it should. Yet, once you notice those imperfections, you start thinking about buying a new one to replace it.

science.title: Using AI to plan your next vacation? Sometimes, too much information is just too much
science.summary: Imagine planning a vacation across India's Golden Triangle: Delhi, Agra and Jaipur. You could compare dozens of websites, scroll through reviews and ask friends for recommendations.

science.title: What faces in paintings can tell us about how we perceive emotion
science.summary: Look closely at a face in a painting and you might think you know what emotion the person is experiencing. A smile suggests happiness. A furrowed brow might signal anger. Widened eyes could mean fear or surprise. But what happens when you ask lots of people the same question? Do they see the same emotion, or something more complicated?

science.title: Serengeti hyenas manage to keep clans stable as climate change alters animal migrations
science.summary: Although the main prey of spotted hyenas (Crocuta crocuta), migratory ungulates such as blue wildebeest (Connochaetes taurinus), now spend substantially less time within hyena territories than they did 30 years ago, hyena clans in the central Serengeti have remained largely stable.

science.title: Subsidence claims: After drought, ground can shrink, swell or even collapse when it rains—causing damage to homes
science.summary: A crack appears beside a window after weeks of scorching weather. As much as you might hope the ground beneath your house will recover with the first rain, the effects of a dry summer can continue long after temperatures fall.

science.title: Ancient fish bones reveal how Arctic cod species survived the last ice age
science.summary: The glacial Arctic Ocean was not a barren ice desert but a breeding ground for the evolution of cold adaptation in marine fish. This is the main conclusion of a new scientific publication from Stockholm University that examines small fish bones found in deep-sea sediments during an expedition aboard the Swedish icebreaker Oden.

science.title: Genetic snapshot of North Carolina black bears could improve population resilience
science.summary: A recent genomic survey of North Carolina black bears from mountain and coastal habitats reveals distinct differences in genetic health and diversity between the populations, with coastal bears exhibiting greater genetic fragility than mountain bears. The results could be used by wildlife management and law enforcement to ensure the health of both bears and the ecosystems they are part of.

science.title: Annual 'Teens and Screens' report reveals young audiences are redefining modern storytelling
science.summary: The media habits of teens and young adults reflect transformative changes in modern storytelling and technology, and the entertainment industry and other content creators should pay attention, according to the latest "Teens and Screens" report from the Center for Scholars & Storytellers (CSS) at UCLA.

science.title: Swiss barn owls are gradually changing color
science.summary: Over the past 30 years, Swiss barn owls have become more reddish-brown and more heavily spotted. By analyzing the genomes of more than 3,000 birds, scientists at the University of Lausanne identified the genetic variants linked to these changes in plumage and revealed natural selection at work. Their findings, published in Nature Communications, show that evolution can happen rapidly in the wild.

science.title: X-ray free-electron laser sets new record for shortest high-energy pulses
science.summary: Researchers at the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS) at the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have measured the shortest high-energy X-ray pulses ever recorded at an X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL). The pulses had photon energies of about 9 kiloelectronvolts (keV) and clocked in at durations of 100 to 400 attoseconds—mere billionths of a billionth of a second. The results are published in Nature Photonics.

science.title: Study identifies world's first corporate psychopath
science.summary: New research suggests the same personality traits associated with toxic corporate leaders today may have been present at the very birth of global capitalism 400 years ago.

science.title: Butterfly navigation tests reveal that migrating species may rely on different natural compasses
science.summary: Researchers at Keele University have discovered that migratory butterflies may use different navigation systems to find their way during migrations, highlighting the importance of understanding how different species may respond to environmental changes.

science.title: Scientists discover migration-mediated mechanism enabling bacteria-virus coexistence
science.summary: Bacteria and the viruses that infect them—known as phages—coexist in soils, oceans and living organisms. Scientists have long thought this coexistence reflects a microscopic version of an evolutionary arms race: As parasites and hosts continually adapt to one another, both evolve ways to survive. But a joint study by researchers at the University of Maryland and the University of Exeter shows different pathways to coexistence.

science.title: Compulsive social media use is linked with wanting closeness but fearing reliance on others
science.summary: Compulsive use of social media may be associated with a strong desire for reassurance among people who are afraid to rely on others and engage in face-to-face interactions, according to a study published Oct. 21, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Chris Bjornsen and Allen Harbaugh of Longwood University in the U.S.

science.title: Electronic nose puts police detection dogs to the test
science.summary: A pilot study tested an electronic nose, called NOS.E, alongside human-remains detection dogs to see whether it could detect buried remains and help confirm dogs' signals.

science.title: Forensic specialists need only one or two facial features to identify individuals
science.summary: Researchers led by Carina Hahn at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), U.S., have found that forensic specialists in facial identification need only one or two features, such as eyes or ears, to identify a face when looking for a match. Published in PLOS One, the study found that specialists find ears to be the most useful but are capable of adapting when recognizing that another feature might be more beneficial.

science.title: Preschoolers aren't more creative than adults—they're just more confident
science.summary: Adults are more objectively creative than preschoolers but are inhibited by anxiety and low self-confidence, according to a study published Oct. 21, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Janika Saretzki from the University of Graz, Austria, and colleagues.

science.title: Chromosome anchors form hollow shells before cell division, imaging reveals
science.summary: Whenever a cell divides, it has to split its chromosomes perfectly between two daughter cells, and even a single mistake can be disastrous. Now, researchers from Japan have found that one of the key structures that makes this possible takes a surprising shape: a hollow sphere.

environment.title: Governors allied with Flávio Bolsonaro set to lead majority of Brazilian Amazon states
environment.summary: Seven of Brazil’s nine Amazonian states are set to be governed by politicians aligned with far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lucas Berti reported for Mongabay Brasil. On Oct. 25, Brazil will have an electoral face-off between the top two candidates for several races that were not able to secure more than 50% of the vote in […]

environment.title: Inside the ‘unique’ tail of Iran’s spider-tailed horned viper
environment.summary: The Iranian spider-tailed horned viper, a rare snake endemic to western Iran, hunts by holding its body completely still while twitching its tail. Its body camouflages among the rocks of its semi-arid Zagros Mountains habitat, but its bulbous tail with accompanying leg-like scales looks remarkably like a large chunky spider. The snake, Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, uses its […]

environment.title: As sand becomes more valuable, Sierra Leone’s Mahera Coast grows more vulnerable
environment.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — When the tide pulls away from the beach in the agricultural regions in Mahera in Lungi, about 27 kilometers (17 miles) across the sea from the country’s capital, Freetown, the digging commences. Young men shovel sand into cement bags and carry them to a flat open area to pile sand […]

environment.title: New Zealand builds an arsenal of tools to battle a ‘wily’ invasive seaweed
environment.summary: BAY OF ISLANDS, Aotearoa New Zealand — Since an invasive seaweed called caulerpa was discovered in Aotearoa New Zealand in 2021, forming meadows that blanketed parts of the seabed, it’s taken on an almost mythical status among people who spend time in coastal waters. “It’s so wily and so resilient,” Michele Rogalin-Henderson, a doctoral candidate […]

environment.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
environment.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

environment.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
environment.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

environment.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
environment.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

environment.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
environment.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

environment.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
environment.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

environment.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
environment.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.

mix_items.title: Vești de la Vatican: Papa Leon nu are nevoie de tratament suplimentar după operația de cancer. Ce spun medicii despre tumora extirpată
mix_items.summary: Medicii papei Leon al XIV-lea confirmă că tumora extirpată în cursul intervenției chirurgicale din 13 octombrie era un adenocarcinom pulmonar și că boala era localizată, nu s-a răspândit, precizând că „nu este necesar niciun tratament suplimentar”, anunță Vatican News.

mix_items.summary: Whenever I drive amid the mazelike bustle of Tokyo's Shuto Expressway, where approximately 1 million vehicles transit daily, I see billboard advertisements for all manner of businesses: dentists, hotels, car and tire companies, and affordable funerals. Lots and lots of funerals.

mix_items.title: Half-matched bone marrow transplant expands options for children with severe aplastic anemia
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center and Johns Hopkins Children's Center report that bone marrow transplant using half-matched family donors achieved a 96% survival rate among child, adolescent and young adult patients with severe aplastic anemia, a rare, life-threatening disorder in which the bone marrow fails to produce enough healthy blood cells. The approach expands access to potentially curative treatment for patients who do not have a fully matched donor.

mix_items.title: Three-week radiation course a safe option for breast cancer patients undergoing reconstruction, trial shows
mix_items.summary: Results of a national clinical trial led by the Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology in conjunction with NRG Oncology and the Canadian Cancer Trials Group show that a shorter, three-week radiation schedule following a mastectomy is as safe and effective as the standard five-week treatment for women undergoing breast reconstruction. The results of the RT CHARM trial (Alliance A221505) are published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

mix_items.summary: rezultatele PISA arată că 48% dintre elevii de 15 ani nu ating nivelul minim de competență la citire deși rezultatele sunt îngrijorătoare, acestea pot fi ameliorate printr-o intervenție integrată și susținută, care să răspundă nevoilor copilului și, totodată, să contribuie la dezvoltarea unei rețele de suport capabile să îi ofere sprijinul necesar pe termen lung […] Articolul Competențele de lectură ale elevilor români scad și este nevoie să intervenim. United Way România implementează un program dedicat literației pentru elevii din medii defavorizate apare prima dată în United Way Romania .

mix_items.title: Salt marshes are proving to be powerful allies in building a climate-resilient coastline
mix_items.summary: Salt marsh sediment and vegetation can remain largely intact even during extreme storm surges. This was demonstrated in a large-scale experiment in which researchers transported sections of salt marsh to an experimental facility capable of producing the world's largest artificial waves. The results show how salt marshes can contribute to natural coastal protection, both in the Netherlands and beyond. The results were published in the journals Nature and Communications Sustainability.

mix_items.title: AI designs functional enzyme components that could help expand drug discovery
mix_items.summary: New active ingredients for drugs to treat infections, cancer or other serious diseases are often based on substances originally discovered in microorganisms, plants or other living organisms. Producing or improving such active ingredients in a targeted manner using microorganisms is often challenging because the underlying biological processes are extremely complex.

mix_items.title: How trustworthy is AI breast cancer detection? New method gauges uncertainty for individual patients
mix_items.summary: While AI offers the ability to improve human experts' ability to diagnose and treat diseases like breast cancer, well-publicized errors across the broader AI field are cause for concern. A team from the University of Pittsburgh has used PSC's flagship Bridges-2 supercomputer to design a deep neural network (DNN) that takes uncertainty into account in diagnosing breast scan images.

mix_items.title: A scuff on your bag, a dent in your mug—and suddenly it feels like time for a new one
mix_items.summary: Imagine you have a bag you really like. It felt like "the one" when you bought it. Over time, it starts to look worn. There are some scuffs on it. Nothing is actually wrong with the bag, and it still works exactly as it should. Yet, once you notice those imperfections, you start thinking about buying a new one to replace it.

mix_items.title: AAO: Association between GLP-1 receptor agonists and age-related macular degeneration explored
mix_items.summary: Crude odds ratios suggest an increased risk for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in association with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) use, but this finding is reversed after adjustment for cardiometabolic confounding variables, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Ophthalmology, held Oct. 9 to 12 in New Orleans.

mix_items.title: After stroke and AFib, restoring heart rhythm linked to lower risk of another stroke
mix_items.summary: For people hospitalized with ischemic stroke and atrial fibrillation (AFib), restoring the heart's normal rhythm within eight weeks after stroke is associated with a lower risk of having another stroke, according to a new study published in Neurology.

mix_items.title: Newer anticoagulants may help prevent strokes in AFib patients with previous brain bleeds
mix_items.summary: For people with atrial fibrillation (AFib), an irregular heartbeat, and intracranial hemorrhage, a type of stroke also known as a brain bleed, anticoagulant use was associated with a lower risk of ischemic stroke and death, according to a new study published in Neurology. The study also found no increased risk of more brain bleeds when people took newer anticoagulants.

mix_items.title: Using AI to plan your next vacation? Sometimes, too much information is just too much
mix_items.summary: Imagine planning a vacation across India's Golden Triangle: Delhi, Agra and Jaipur. You could compare dozens of websites, scroll through reviews and ask friends for recommendations.

mix_items.title: What faces in paintings can tell us about how we perceive emotion
mix_items.summary: Look closely at a face in a painting and you might think you know what emotion the person is experiencing. A smile suggests happiness. A furrowed brow might signal anger. Widened eyes could mean fear or surprise. But what happens when you ask lots of people the same question? Do they see the same emotion, or something more complicated?

mix_items.title: Air pollution and temperature variability are associated with higher blood glucose levels
mix_items.summary: A European study involving GCAT identifies associations between air pollution, temperature variability and blood glucose levels in people without diabetes.

mix_items.title: Serengeti hyenas manage to keep clans stable as climate change alters animal migrations
mix_items.summary: Although the main prey of spotted hyenas (Crocuta crocuta), migratory ungulates such as blue wildebeest (Connochaetes taurinus), now spend substantially less time within hyena territories than they did 30 years ago, hyena clans in the central Serengeti have remained largely stable.

mix_items.title: Personalized medicine breakthrough for childhood leukemia
mix_items.summary: Researchers from Newcastle University and Great Ormond Street Hospital have identified new predictors of relapse in children and young people with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) treated with the immunotherapy drug blinatumomab, as part of a U.K.-wide study.

mix_items.title: Subsidence claims: After drought, ground can shrink, swell or even collapse when it rains—causing damage to homes
mix_items.summary: A crack appears beside a window after weeks of scorching weather. As much as you might hope the ground beneath your house will recover with the first rain, the effects of a dry summer can continue long after temperatures fall.

mix_items.title: STI rates drop following antibiotic use recommendations for gay and bisexual men
mix_items.summary: After years of rising sexually transmitted infection (STI) rates in Australia, new Burnet Institute–led research has found promising evidence that an existing antibiotic taken after sex may be helping to reduce syphilis and chlamydia diagnoses among gay and bisexual men.

mix_items.title: Ancient fish bones reveal how Arctic cod species survived the last ice age
mix_items.summary: The glacial Arctic Ocean was not a barren ice desert but a breeding ground for the evolution of cold adaptation in marine fish. This is the main conclusion of a new scientific publication from Stockholm University that examines small fish bones found in deep-sea sediments during an expedition aboard the Swedish icebreaker Oden.

mix_items.title: Genetic snapshot of North Carolina black bears could improve population resilience
mix_items.summary: A recent genomic survey of North Carolina black bears from mountain and coastal habitats reveals distinct differences in genetic health and diversity between the populations, with coastal bears exhibiting greater genetic fragility than mountain bears. The results could be used by wildlife management and law enforcement to ensure the health of both bears and the ecosystems they are part of.

mix_items.title: Annual 'Teens and Screens' report reveals young audiences are redefining modern storytelling
mix_items.summary: The media habits of teens and young adults reflect transformative changes in modern storytelling and technology, and the entertainment industry and other content creators should pay attention, according to the latest "Teens and Screens" report from the Center for Scholars & Storytellers (CSS) at UCLA.

mix_items.title: Swiss barn owls are gradually changing color
mix_items.summary: Over the past 30 years, Swiss barn owls have become more reddish-brown and more heavily spotted. By analyzing the genomes of more than 3,000 birds, scientists at the University of Lausanne identified the genetic variants linked to these changes in plumage and revealed natural selection at work. Their findings, published in Nature Communications, show that evolution can happen rapidly in the wild.

mix_items.title: Study finds health care provider photos in waiting rooms can strengthen patient trust
mix_items.summary: A new Florida State University study finds that adding health care providers' photographs to clinic welcome signs can strengthen certain aspects of patient trust before patients even meet their providers.

mix_items.title: Pancreatic cancer study highlights body's natural molecules as potential treatment tools
mix_items.summary: Pancreatic cancer cells are remarkably good at doing one thing: growing. But new Texas A&M research suggests that two tiny molecules already present in the body may help slow them down.

mix_items.title: X-ray free-electron laser sets new record for shortest high-energy pulses
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS) at the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have measured the shortest high-energy X-ray pulses ever recorded at an X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL). The pulses had photon energies of about 9 kiloelectronvolts (keV) and clocked in at durations of 100 to 400 attoseconds—mere billionths of a billionth of a second. The results are published in Nature Photonics.

mix_items.title: Study identifies world's first corporate psychopath
mix_items.summary: New research suggests the same personality traits associated with toxic corporate leaders today may have been present at the very birth of global capitalism 400 years ago.

mix_items.title: Blood proteins could reveal clues to prostate cancer risk more than a decade before diagnosis
mix_items.summary: Proteins linked to the immune system, cell adhesion, blood vessel formation and known prostate cancer genes were associated with the future risk of developing prostate cancer, including aggressive disease, in a new study led by researchers at Oxford Population Health.

mix_items.title: Wearable pressure sensor uses cold-spray adhesion method for enhanced health monitoring
mix_items.summary: In a potential advance for wearable technology, researchers from Virginia Commonwealth University and Florida International University have developed a cold-spray technique that can reliably deposit sensors directly onto human skin and other flexible surfaces.

mix_items.title: Butterfly navigation tests reveal that migrating species may rely on different natural compasses
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Keele University have discovered that migratory butterflies may use different navigation systems to find their way during migrations, highlighting the importance of understanding how different species may respond to environmental changes.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover migration-mediated mechanism enabling bacteria-virus coexistence
mix_items.summary: Bacteria and the viruses that infect them—known as phages—coexist in soils, oceans and living organisms. Scientists have long thought this coexistence reflects a microscopic version of an evolutionary arms race: As parasites and hosts continually adapt to one another, both evolve ways to survive. But a joint study by researchers at the University of Maryland and the University of Exeter shows different pathways to coexistence.

mix_items.title: Compulsive social media use is linked with wanting closeness but fearing reliance on others
mix_items.summary: Compulsive use of social media may be associated with a strong desire for reassurance among people who are afraid to rely on others and engage in face-to-face interactions, according to a study published Oct. 21, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Chris Bjornsen and Allen Harbaugh of Longwood University in the U.S.

mix_items.title: Experimental treatment selectively reduces harmful protein in lab models of rare inherited brain disorder
mix_items.summary: Researchers from DZNE and the Hertie Institute for Clinical Brain Research (HIH) at the University of Tübingen, together with experts from Bonn, London and Portugal, have developed and successfully tested in human neurons cultured in the lab a new approach for treating the rare neurodegenerative disease spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3).

mix_items.title: Existing cancer drug reduces blood vessel malformations in the brain
mix_items.summary: Researchers have identified a substance that reduces blood vessel lesions in the brain in the disease cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM). The substance is already used to treat brain tumors in children and could therefore be repurposed relatively rapidly to treat CCM, hopefully replacing surgery, currently the only treatment option.

mix_items.title: Tuberculosis vaccine's link to reduced dementia risk gains mechanistic support
mix_items.summary: Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG), a vaccine widely used to prevent tuberculosis and treat bladder cancer, may also have properties that reduce the risk for dementia, according to new findings in a study of mice. BCG is a live, weakened vaccine made from an altered strain of the bacterium Mycobacterium bovis.

mix_items.title: Electronic nose puts police detection dogs to the test
mix_items.summary: A pilot study tested an electronic nose, called NOS.E, alongside human-remains detection dogs to see whether it could detect buried remains and help confirm dogs' signals.

mix_items.title: Forensic specialists need only one or two facial features to identify individuals
mix_items.summary: Researchers led by Carina Hahn at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), U.S., have found that forensic specialists in facial identification need only one or two features, such as eyes or ears, to identify a face when looking for a match. Published in PLOS One, the study found that specialists find ears to be the most useful but are capable of adapting when recognizing that another feature might be more beneficial.

mix_items.title: Preschoolers aren't more creative than adults—they're just more confident
mix_items.summary: Adults are more objectively creative than preschoolers but are inhibited by anxiety and low self-confidence, according to a study published Oct. 21, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Janika Saretzki from the University of Graz, Austria, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Chromosome anchors form hollow shells before cell division, imaging reveals
mix_items.summary: Whenever a cell divides, it has to split its chromosomes perfectly between two daughter cells, and even a single mistake can be disastrous. Now, researchers from Japan have found that one of the key structures that makes this possible takes a surprising shape: a hollow sphere.

mix_items.title: 'Digital twins' of immune system in pregnancy identify drugs to prevent early labor
mix_items.summary: Researchers have identified two common drugs that may, when given together during pregnancy, prevent premature births. The finding is the fruit of a new Stanford Medicine–led, artificial intelligence–powered technique for screening drugs to prevent early labor. It uses a comprehensive atlas of the immune system, which the researchers built to be accurate at a cell-by-cell level, to create "digital twins" of the immune systems of individual pregnant women for virtual drug testing.

mix_items.title: Modifiable psychosocial factors linked to depression among US cancer survivors
mix_items.summary: Loneliness, functional limitations and lack of social support were independently associated with depression in a large U.S.-based study of cancer survivors by Philip Baiden from The University of Texas Arlington, U.S., and colleagues, published Oct. 21, 2026, in the PLOS One.

mix_items.title: Governors allied with Flávio Bolsonaro set to lead majority of Brazilian Amazon states
mix_items.summary: Seven of Brazil’s nine Amazonian states are set to be governed by politicians aligned with far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lucas Berti reported for Mongabay Brasil. On Oct. 25, Brazil will have an electoral face-off between the top two candidates for several races that were not able to secure more than 50% of the vote in […]

mix_items.title: Inside the ‘unique’ tail of Iran’s spider-tailed horned viper
mix_items.summary: The Iranian spider-tailed horned viper, a rare snake endemic to western Iran, hunts by holding its body completely still while twitching its tail. Its body camouflages among the rocks of its semi-arid Zagros Mountains habitat, but its bulbous tail with accompanying leg-like scales looks remarkably like a large chunky spider. mix_items.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
mix_items.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

mix_items.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
mix_items.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

mix_items.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
mix_items.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

mix_items.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
mix_items.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

mix_items.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
mix_items.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

mix_items.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.
